About

How I work

I am a Technical Game Designer in Rio de Janeiro. I design gameplay systems — economies, progression, balance, level layouts — and then I build them in Unity myself.

That combination is the point. On Memories of War I was hired as the programmer and ended up renegotiating the design with the client, because I was the one watching it fail. On Cursed Blight I had two days to write a design document for a game I then had to build alone in a month, so I designed only what I knew I could ship. On All Stars Merge I shipped features into a codebase dozens of people had passed through without agreeing on a structure.

Right now I am leading a four-person programming team at UFF Media Lab on an educational VR project about the Atlantic slave trade, built with the university's history institute and a UNESCO Chair. My job there is as much translation as engineering: turning what historians need into something that works in a headset.

I have worked remotely since 2022, in English, every day. I am certified C1 and I teach English to three students, so the working language of a distributed team is not a risk with me. I am in UTC−3, which overlaps a full working day with Europe and most of one with the Americas.

Away from work I play video games in chronological order from 1947, run tabletop RPGs and design my own. I think games are an art medium that can genuinely help people, and I would like to keep making ones worth someone's time.

Beyond the screen

Two long-running side projects

Not games I shipped, but directly the reason I design the way I do.

A 2d10 tabletop RPG system

I am designing my own tabletop RPG from the ground up — balancing mechanics, economy and progression through spreadsheet modelling, then playtesting with real players and iterating on their feedback. It is the same work as balancing a video game, with the numbers fully exposed.

Core system Balance tables Rules document

Playing the history of video games in order

I am working through the culturally significant games of every era in chronological order, starting from 1947, and documenting them as I go. It is a slow way to build real literacy in the medium — knowing why a mechanic exists, not just that it does. The backlog is close to infinite.
